figures.caption: Figure 1: Reconstruction of seen image by NeuroRefine. Each pair shows the seen image (left) and our reconstruction (right), using the full NSD dataset (40 hours) for subject 1. The low-level branch supplies a spatial prior, six one-hidden-layer MLP heads predict the content prompt, and the frozen Qwen-Image-Edit2511 refiner restores texture, colour and sharpness.

Figure 2: Overview of NeuroRefine. fMRI betas (39,548 fsaverage surface vertices) feed two pathways. (A) Low-level / spatial pathway: a per-subject VGG feature readout trained with InfoNCE predicts multi-layer VGG features, which a Deep Image Prior inverts into a low-level image that supplies the coarse spatial layout. (B) Content pathway: six independent MLP heads (scene, subject, count, colour, object, layout; 1024 units, GELU, dropout 0.3) predict structured content that is assembled into a content prompt. The frozen Qwen-Image-Edit-2511 editor takes the low-level image as an image condition and the content prompt as text, and returns a 1024× 1024 reconstruction (20 steps, cfg 4.0). Unlike Brain-IT (Beliy et al., 2026), which conditions its SDXL refiner on a caption, NeuroRefine conditions the refiner on the low-level image itself. Lower panels: head attribution on the surface and the evaluation protocol.

Figure 3: Stages of the pipeline. Rows are concepts where NeuroRefine wins; columns are the seen image, the low-level image, Brain-IT semantic, Brain-IT enhanced, caption+Qwen, retrieval+Qwen and NeuroRefine.

Figure 4: Same generator, different conditioning. Qwen-Image-Edit conditioned on the fMRIdecoded caption, on the ground-truth caption, and on the fMRI-derived low-level image with the head content prompt.

Table 1: Quantitative comparison. Top block: prior numbers as reported by Brain-IT (Beliy et al., 2026) for methods trained on the full 40 h of NSD data, averaged over subjects 1,2,5,7. Bottom block: NeuroRefine, measured by us with the same compute_metrics code on the identical 930 shared-concept ground truth for subject 1 (LPIPS is omitted by the released code). The two blocks therefore differ in subject coverage: the prior numbers are four-subject averages as reported by BrainIT, whereas our row is a single-subject measurement and should be read as such. The panel is multifactor (low-level: PixCorr/SSIM/Alex(2); semantic: Inception/CLIP/EffNet/SwAV); we report both factors and do not collapse them into one number (Sec. 5.1). Best per column in bold, second best underlined; arrows give the direction of improvement.

Figure 5: Retrieval as conditioning. The retrieved photograph carries the right content in a different arrangement; conditioning on the low-level image instead retains far more of the input arrangement.

Figure 6: Subject-1 reconstructions on four of the shared concepts: seen image, low-level input, Brain-IT enhanced and NeuroRefine. The cross-subject comparison is quantitative (table 3); persubject head-prompt renders exist for subject 1 only, so this figure shows subject 1.
Figure 7: Where does subject data go? (a) CLIP image cosine of the readout against the number of subject-1 images, with and without cross-subject initialisation; (b) retrieval top-1.

Figure 8: Low-level versus semantic factor across arms. The factors are not redundant: the blurriest arm is high on PixCorr and low on CLIP cosine, and the sharp arms spread along the semantic axis; no single arm dominates both axes.
Figure 9: Head attribution on the inflated fsaverage surface (saliency, row-normalised per head; top row left hemisphere, bottom row right hemisphere). All six heads load on visual cortex.
Figure 10: Causal lesion test. Change in head logits when the top-5% salient vertices are zeroed, relative to a random 5% (dots: individual subjects).

Figure 11: Failure modes, one row per type. Object substitution: a bird on a wire becomes an airplane (c226). Instance/species substitution: a giraffe becomes a zebra (c832). Scene substitution: a fruit basket becomes an indoor scene with a person (c97). Scene and count together: two red vases become a room with two people (c563). Count: a crowded race field becomes a single rider in a forest (c331). Direction: a walker under a red umbrella becomes a frontal standing figure (c264). Columns: seen image, low-level input, Brain-IT enhanced, NeuroRefine.
Figure 12: Qualitative comparison (1/2): 14 of the 28 concepts used in the main figures. Columns are the seen image, the low-level input, Brain-IT enhanced and NeuroRefine.

Figure 13: Retrieval semantic stage. The retrieved photograph (4th column) is a real image with the right content but a different arrangement; the edit refiner (last) keeps the retrieved content and recovers some layout from the low-level input.
